title: Endives braisées
subtitle: Buttery braised Belgian endive with lemon and sugar
excerpt: Belgian endive halves braised in butter, lemon juice, and a little stock until golden outside and soft and slightly sweet within. The bitter edge of raw endive disappears; what remains is nutty and caramelised.
sourceNotes: Braised endive (endives braisées) is a classic of French and Belgian cookery documented in Larousse Gastronomique (1938) and in Prosper Montagné's broader culinary writings. The braising method for chicory/endive is standard in French vegetable cookery.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Can be braised an hour ahead and kept warm. Re-caramelise briefly in a pan before serving if needed.

content.text: Endives braisées transforms raw Belgian endive, which is bitter and squeaky, into something entirely different: soft, caramelised, and barely bitter at all. The lemon juice stops them from turning completely sweet; the butter and the slow cooking do the rest. Serve alongside roast chicken, duck, or a piece of grilled pork.

Heat 30 g of the butter in a wide, heavy saucepan or ovenproof sauté pan over medium-high heat. When foaming, lay the endive halves cut-side down in the pan. Cook for 4 to 5 minutes without moving until golden brown on the cut side. Turn and cook for 2 minutes on the other side.

Sprinkle the sugar over the endives. Add the lemon juice and stock. The liquid will bubble and splutter. Reduce the heat to low. Cut a circle of greaseproof paper to fit inside the pan and lay it directly on top of the endives. Cover the pan with a lid or foil.

Braise over a very low heat for 25 to 30 minutes until the endives are completely tender when pierced with a knife. Lift out onto a warm plate. Add the remaining 20 g of butter to the braising liquid, raise the heat, and reduce to a syrupy glaze. Pour over the endives and serve.

items.symptom: Endives are still firm after 30 minutes
items.cause: Heat too low, or endives were very large
items.fix: Add a splash more stock and continue braising, covered, until tender. Large endives can take 40 minutes.

items.cause: Under-braised; the bitterness needs the slow cooking to mellow
items.fix: Braise longer and more gently. The lemon juice also helps; make sure you have not skipped it.

content.text: Braised endive is eaten throughout northern France and Belgium, where endive (chicorée witloof) is a major commercial crop grown in the Pas-de-Calais and Picardy. It is a winter vegetable, and the classic winter preparation is either braised in the pan or, in the Belgian tradition, wrapped in ham and baked in béchamel. Both are classics of the northern French winter table. Endives braisées is the simpler of the two, and easier to serve alongside other dishes without the béchamel taking over.
